qs.q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle do the aortic and pulmonary valves open?
qs.e: The aortic and pulmonary valves (semilunar valves) open during ventricular ejection. This phase begins when the pressure in the ventricles exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery, forcing blood out of the ventricles. Atrial systole (A) is when atria contract. ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The cardiac cycle is the repeating sequence of electrical and mechanical events that fill the heart and eject blood. Understanding timing, pressures and sounds links physiology to bedside assessment.

sections.p: Each heartbeat consists of atrial contraction, ventricular contraction, ejection, and relaxation. These phases generate the four classic heart sounds and define systolic and diastolic periods.
b: Four phases: atrial systole, isovolumic contraction, ventricular ejection, isovolumic relaxation.
Heart sounds: S1 (closure of AV valves), S2 (closure of semilunar valves), S3 and S4 (rare, indicate filling abnormalities).

sections.p: Electrical depolarization (P wave → QRS → T wave) triggers muscle contraction. Pressure rises in the ventricles before the semilunar valves open, then falls as blood is ejected.
b: Atrial systole adds ~20% of ventricular end‑diastolic volume.
Isovolumic phases generate pressure without volume change, crucial for valve timing.

t.b: What phase of the cycle is occurring? Shows timing of depolarization (P, QRS, T) and helps estimate QT interval.
Which heart sound is present? Identifies valve closure and abnormal filling (e.g., S3 in heart failure).
How is ventricular filling/ejection fraction? Visualizes wall motion and valve function when ECG or stethoscope are inconclusive.

sections.p: Autonomic input, baroreceptor reflexes, and circulating hormones adjust heart rate and contractility to match metabolic demand.
b: Parasympathetic ↑ vagal tone, lengthen diastole, lower HR.

sections.p: Disruption of timing or pressure gradients leads to murmurs, heart failure, or arrhythmias. Common low‑resource causes include rheumatic valve disease, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy, and malaria‑induced anemia.
b: Valve stenosis → prolonged ejection time, louder S1/S2.
Heart failure → reduced ejection fraction, presence of S3.

sections.p: Recognizing abnormal sounds, pulse pressure changes, and ECG patterns guides urgent management of shock, acute valve rupture, or decompensated heart failure.
b: Narrow pulse pressure → aortic stenosis or hypovolemia.
Wide pulse pressure → aortic regurgitation or sepsis.

t.b: What is pulse pressure? Helps infer stroke volume and valve competence.
What cardiac silhouette size? Detects cardiomegaly from chronic volume overload.

sections.p: Focus on the sequence of sounds, pressure changes, and ECG intervals. Relate each to the underlying mechanical phase.
b: S1 occurs at end of isovolumic contraction; S2 at start of isovolumic relaxation.
QT interval shortens with tachycardia; ≈40% of cycle at normal HR.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute chest pain with new murmur (possible valve rupture)
Sudden severe dyspnea with S3 (acute decompensated heart failure)
Syncope with rapid tachyarrhythmia (risk of cardiac arrest)

faq.q: Why does tachycardia reduce cardiac output?
faq.a: Faster rates shorten diastole, limiting ventricular filling and stroke volume.

faq.q: What does an S4 sound indicate?
faq.a: A stiff ventricle that atria must forcefully contract against, seen in hypertrophy or ischemia.

faq.q: How is the QT interval related to the cardiac cycle?
faq.a: It spans ventricular depolarization to repolarization; a shorter QT reflects a faster heart rate.

exam: Explain how the four heart sounds correspond to phases of the cardiac cycle.
Interpret a shortened QT interval on ECG in a patient with tachycardia.
Describe the hemodynamic changes in aortic stenosis and how they affect pulse pressure.
